title: Uber Shuttle Seat Allocation
statement:
An Uber shuttle has `n` seats in a single row, numbered `0` to `n - 1`. Riders board and leave one at a time.

When a rider boards, they choose the seat that maximises the distance to the **nearest** rider already seated. The distance between seats `a` and `b` is `|a - b|`. The rules are:

- If the shuttle is empty, the rider takes seat `0`.
- Otherwise the rider picks, among all free seats, the one whose distance to the closest occupied seat is largest. A free seat at either end of the row only has a neighbour on one side, so that distance is measured to that single neighbour.
- If several seats give the same largest distance, the rider takes the one with the **lowest seat number**.

When a rider drops off, their seat becomes free.

Simulate the shuttle by implementing the class `UberShuttle`:

- `UberShuttle(n)` creates a shuttle with `n` seats.
- `board()` seats the next rider by the rules above and returns the seat number.
- `dropOff(p)` frees seat `p`, which is guaranteed to be occupied at that moment.

It is guaranteed that `board()` is only called when at least one seat is free.

**Follow-up:** `n` can be as large as `10^9`, so you cannot keep an array of seats, and a `board()` call that scans all occupied seats is too slow.
input_format:
The first line contains two integers `n` and `q`: the number of seats and the number of operations.
Each of the next `q` lines is either `board` or `dropOff p`, in the order they are performed.
output_format: For every `board` operation, in order, print the returned seat number on its own line. `dropOff` operations print nothing. If there is no `board` operation, print nothing.
constraints: `board` is only issued while a seat is free; `dropOff p` is only issued for an occupied seat `p`

examples.input:
10 6
board
board
board
board
dropOff 0
board
examples.explanation: The first rider takes seat 0 and the second takes the far end, seat 9. The third picks the middle of the gap, seat 4 (distance 4). The fourth faces two gaps, (0, 4) and (4, 9). Seat 2 has distance 2 to its neighbours, and so do seats 6 and 7 in the other gap, so the lowest, seat 2, wins. After the rider in seat 0 leaves, seat 0 itself has distance 2 to seat 2, seat 6 also has distance 2, and the lowest number, 0, is chosen.
Seats 0 and 4 are taken first. After seat 0 is freed, the next rider sits at the end seat 0 again (distance 4 from seat 4). The last rider takes the middle of the gap between seats 0 and 4, seat 2.

hints: Between two neighbouring occupied seats `l` and `r`, the best free seat is the middle one (the lower middle on ties), at distance `(r - l) / 2`. At the two ends of the row the best seat is the end seat itself.
Keep the gaps between occupied seats in a max-heap keyed by (best distance, then lowest seat), and keep a way to find a seat's left and right occupied neighbours (for example linked-list style maps).
On a drop-off, two gaps merge into one. Rather than deleting the two old gaps from the heap, push the new gap and skip stale heap entries when you pop them.
